extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing science fiction authors / fiction writers seeking world-building advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for constructing believable, immersive science fiction worlds that support plot, theme, and character. The page lists concrete aspects authors should design (concept, rules, cultures, geography, history, character use) with examples from classic SF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a Strong Concept
rubrics_metrics.description: World-building requires you to build a sandbox for your characters to play in – but it has to be starkly different from our own. Effective world-building in science fiction usually begins by identifying a central concept to skew – something different about this new world that serves as the foundation for making your entire universe feel alien.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a central, striking idea (a technological innovation, an alternate reality, or a unique event affecting the characters) that will shape rules, culture, and social dynamics. A strong concept engages readers and provides coherent reasons for the world's peculiarities. Example given: Philip K. Dick’s Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? — the concept of humanoid androids blurring man/machine boundaries sets ethical questions and societal norms for the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in Rules and Laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-built science fiction world adheres to a set of internal rules and laws that govern its functioning – and a good author never strays from them!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the world's rules (physics, technology, biology, or systems of 'magic') and maintain them consistently so readers can rely on them to make sense of characters' motivations and plot developments. Inconsistency undermines believability. Example: Isaac Asimov’s Foundation series uses the consistent concept of 'psychohistory' to justify societal behavior and plot logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural Diversity and Societal Structures
rubrics_metrics.description: The best science fiction features richly developed worlds that include diverse cultures, societies, and hierarchies, which add depth, foster a sense of 'otherness', and create opportunities to explore themes like identity and power dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design distinct cultures, social norms, and hierarchical structures to enrich the world and enable thematic exploration (e.g., of identity or politics) without direct real-world confrontation. Use cultural contrasts to make the world feel lived-in and to interrogate social issues. Example: Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Left Hand of Darkness — an androgynous society challenges our notions of gender and shows how societal norms shape individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed Geography and Setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive geography and an immersive setting contribute to the overall realism of your science fiction world and help readers feel like they’re really there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop coherent, consistent physical environments (landscapes, cities, ecosystems) and use sensory details (smells, sensations, sounds) to immerse readers. Geography should influence culture and plot; treat the setting as a character when appropriate. Example: Frank Herbert’s Dune — the desert world of Arrakis (sandworms, spice, harsh environment) creates a 'sense of place' essential to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate Historical and Societal Contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding historical and societal details within the science fiction world helps lend authenticity and depth, and allows authors to mirror real-world issues safely within fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create histories, past events, institutions, and societal developments that explain why towns, cultures, and politics are as they are. Use fictional history to give weight to current conflicts and to enable parallels with real-world problems. Example: Octavia Butler’s Kindred blends historical context (antebellum slavery) with SF to explore enduring social issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as Vessels of Exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use well-developed characters as the vehicles through which readers can explore the intricacies of the science fiction world; avoid building worlds at the expense of character development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters have compelling motivations grounded in the world's context so their perspectives reveal world details naturally. Anchor exposition in character experience rather than info-dump. Anti-pattern: overemphasizing world detail while neglecting character depth. Example: Orson Scott Card’s Ender’s Game uses Ender’s experiences to expose political tensions, technology, and ethical dilemmas.
